conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I know you can't speak, but I'm here to help. You were brought in because you weren’t responding at the nursing home. We’re going to take good care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low and your oxygen levels were down. We think you have an infection, possibly from your lungs or your urinary tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started antibiotics through your IV. We also did a CT scan of your head—no stroke or bleeding. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some new shadows in your lungs. Could be pneumonia. But your urine was also cloudy and smelly—so we’re treating both possibilities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a trach mask for oxygen. We’ll keep monitoring your breathing and blood pressure closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work shows your white count is high—sign of infection. Lactate is elevated too, which means your body isn’t perfusing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think you’re in septic shock. That’s why your blood pressure dropped. We gave fluids and you’re a bit more stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidneys are stressed—creatinine is up. But it’s likely from low blood flow, not permanent damage. We’re watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing broad antibiotics—meropenem and vancomycin—for now. We’ll adjust once we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the right lung collapse has worsened. We’re doing more suctioning through your trach to clear secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also increasing your breathing treatments. You’re still on antibiotics and fluids. Your blood pressure is better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good update—your latest labs show your kidney function is improving. Creatinine is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture grew Proteus mirabilis. That’s a bacteria we’ve seen in your past infections. It’s sensitive to meropenem, so we’ll keep that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping ciprofloxacin since we don’t think there’s a resistant strain this time. Vancomycin stays for broader coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are still negative after 48 hours—that’s reassuring. Less likely to be widespread bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re looking better. You’re more responsive—nodding when asked questions. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are stable on the trach mask. The lung collapse is improving. We’re encouraged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line today so you can finish antibiotics outside the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line is in. It goes into a vein in your arm and up to a large vein near your heart. It’s for long-term antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The first X-ray showed it was too far in—into the right atrium. But we’ve pulled it back. Now it’s in the right spot—mid superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get meropenem every 8 hours and vancomycin every 12 through this line for 5 more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your INR today—it’s 3.8. That means your blood is too thin. We’re holding warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t want you to bleed, especially since you had a central line placed. We’ll restart warfarin when your INR is safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sacral ulcers are healing—good granulation tissue, no infection. We’ll keep using the zinc oxide and reposition you regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family and I talked about your care goals. We’ve updated your status to DNR—but you can still be ventilated through your trach if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This means if your heart stops, we won’t do CPR, but we will support your breathing if it’s temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day—we’re getting ready to discharge you to extended care. You’ve done really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your infection is under control. Blood pressure and oxygen are stable. Kidney function has returned to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish your antibiotics at the facility. The PICC line will stay in for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll check a vancomycin level tomorrow—before your fourth dose. That’s important to avoid side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Warfarin is on hold. They’ll check your INR again soon and restart it when it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diabetes is stable. Keep on the same insulin doses. We’re switching your duloxetine to Paxil—it’s easier to give through your feeding tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your other meds are continuing—gabapentin, fentanyl patch, levothyroxine, lansoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any questions? I know you can’t ask, but if your family has concerns, now’s the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just nod if you understand. We’re making sure everything’s clear before you go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still bedbound and nonverbal, but you’re alert and responding. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing your breathing treatments. Stay hydrated. And we’ll follow up with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve fought through a tough infection. You’re stronger now. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your new facility has all the instructions. They’ll take great care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going to be okay. Rest well, and keep fighting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up if needed. For now, just focus on healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re discharging you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check—your vitals are great. Heart rate 84, BP 128 over 72, oxygen 97% on trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Foley draining clear urine—no more pus. That means the UTI is clearing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Extremities warm—good sign your circulation is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident you’re ready for the next step. You’ve come a long way in three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a few more papers, and you’ll be on your way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember—vancomycin trough tomorrow morning. Before the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And no warfarin until INR is checked and safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re doing great. We’ll miss you, but you’re ready.
